input: This appraisal examines the financial case for a proposed warehouse extension. The installed cost of the extension is $790k, and the expected net saving is $203k per year over a period of 12 years. Discounting the savings at a rate of 8% gives a present value of $1530k, and subtracting the installed cost leads to a net present value of $740k, which is comfortably positive. On a simple payback basis, the installed cost is recovered in 3.89 years, after which the savings continue to accrue for the remainder of the appraisal period. The mechanics of the calculation are straightforward: each year's saving is worth progressively less in present-value terms the further it lies in the future, and the discount rate captures that effect across the whole period under consideration. If the savings were to fall short of the estimates, the net present value would fall correspondingly, because a shortfall in any one year is repeated, in effect, across every year of the period. These figures suggest that the extension represents an attractive investment that would strengthen the logistics position of the operation. It is important to note, however, that the savings figures are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the appraisal should be read as an indication of the potential return rather than as a firm prediction of the outcome that will actually be achieved once the extension has been built and has entered service.
target: The warehouse extension has a net present value of $740k on the stated estimates. The installed cost is $790k. The expected net saving is $203k per year for 12 years, and at a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $1530k. The net present value is the present value of the savings less the installed cost: it states what the stream of savings is worth today, over and above the cost of obtaining it, with each year's saving discounted for the wait until it arrives. The margin is wide. The savings could fall well short of the estimate before the present value of the savings came down to the installed cost and the appraisal turned negative. On a simple payback basis the installed cost is recovered in 3.89 years, inside the first part of the appraisal period, and the savings of the remaining years are then return rather than recovery. The payback figure takes no account of discounting and is the weaker of the two measures; it is stated because it shows how long the capital is exposed before it is recovered, which the present-value figure does not show directly. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, and the appraisal inherits that uncertainty in full: the discounting arithmetic is exact, but its largest input is an estimate, and a measured saving from a comparable extension would replace the weakest figure in the case. The decision the figures support is to proceed on the estimates as stated, with the saving treated as unproven until the extension has operated. If the realised saving matches the estimate, the return is as appraised; if it falls short, the net present value falls with it, year by year, across the whole period.
